files.README.md:
# Freelance Client Pipeline Kit

Stop the feast-and-famine cycle. This kit gives you a simple, repeatable way
to find, pitch and follow up with new clients in about three hours a week,
so the next project is lined up before the current one ends.

## What's inside

| File | What it's for | Time needed |
|---|---|---|
| ideal-client-profile.md | Decide exactly who you're looking for, with a completed example | 30 min, once |
| lead-sources.md | Ten places to find clients, ranked by effort and how fast they pay off | 15 min read |
| outreach-emails.md | Ten emails: past clients, referrals, warm intros, cold pitches and follow-ups | Copy as needed |
| pipeline-tracker.csv | Track every lead from first contact to signed, with example rows | 2 min per lead |
| pipeline-maths.md | Work out how many conversations you need each month, with worked maths | 20 min, once |
| weekly-prospecting-routine.md | A three-hour weekly routine, split into short daily blocks | 3 hours a week |

## How to use it

1. **Know who you want.** Fill in the ideal client profile. A clear profile
   makes every other step faster: you know where to look and what to say.
2. **Do the maths.** Use pipeline-maths.md to turn your income target into
   a number of conversations per week. Most freelancers are surprised how
   small, and how steady, the number is.
3. **Start with warm leads.** Before any cold outreach, work through the
   "warm first" list in lead-sources.md: past clients, people who referred
   you before, and your existing network. These convert far better.
4. **Track everything.** Every lead goes in pipeline-tracker.csv the day you
   contact them, with a "next action" and a date. If it isn't in the
   tracker, it will be forgotten.
5. **Keep the routine.** Block the weekly routine in your calendar, and keep
   doing it when you're busy. The routine is what ends feast-and-famine:
   the clients you pitch this month are next month's work.

## Opening the tracker

pipeline-tracker.csv opens in any spreadsheet app (Excel, Google Sheets,
Numbers, LibreOffice). Delete the example rows when you're ready, or keep
them as a guide. Sort by "next_action_date" each morning to see who to
contact today.

## A note on expectations

No template guarantees replies. What this kit does is make outreach
consistent, personal and easy to keep up, which is what makes the
difference over a few months. Adapt every email to the person you're
writing to; a message that clearly couldn't have been sent to anyone else
is the one that gets answered.

# Ideal Client Profile

A one-page description of the client you most want more of. Fill it in
once, review it every quarter.

## Step 1: Look back before you look forward

List your last 5-10 clients and score each from 1 (poor) to 5 (great):

| Client | Paid on time? | Good rate? | Easy to work with? | Work you enjoy? | Led to more work? | Total /25 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |

Circle the top two or three. Your profile should describe *those* clients,
not the average one.

## Step 2: Fill in the profile

**Type of organisation:** (industry, size, stage)

**The person who hires you:** (job title, what they're responsible for)

**The problem they have when they need you:** (in their words, not yours)

**What triggers the need:** (an event that makes them start looking: a
launch, a new hire, a funding round, a busy season, a deadline)

**What they've usually tried already:**

**Budget range for a typical project:**

**Where they spend time / who they listen to:** (events, groups, newsletters,
communities, other suppliers)

**Signs they're a good fit:**

**Signs to walk away:**

**One sentence I can use to describe who I help:**
"I help [who] [get what result] [without what pain]."

## Completed example

*A freelance copywriter who writes website and email copy.*

**Type of organisation:** Independent service businesses with 2-15 staff:
physiotherapy and wellness clinics, accountants, small architecture studios.

**The person who hires you:** The owner, or an office manager who has been
handed "the website" on top of their real job.

**The problem they have when they need you:** "Our website doesn't say what
we actually do, and nobody books from it." "We send a newsletter but no one
reads it."

**What triggers the need:** A website rebuild, opening a second location,
taking on a new partner, or the slow months after a busy season.

**What they've usually tried already:** Writing it themselves on a weekend,
or using whatever the web designer put in as placeholder text.

**Budget range for a typical project:** $1,500-$4,000 for website copy;
$400-$800 a month for a newsletter.

**Where they spend time / who they listen to:** Local business groups,
their professional association, their accountant and web designer.

**Signs they're a good fit:** They already have clients and a clear
service; they've set aside budget; one person can approve the work.

**Signs to walk away:** "We just need a few words, should be quick."
Five people need to approve every page. They want copy before they've
decided what services they offer.

**One sentence:** "I help small clinics and professional practices turn
their website into something that books appointments, without the owner
having to write a word."

## Step 3: Use it

- Read your one-sentence description out loud. If a stranger can't tell
  whether they're a fit, make it narrower.
- Use "what triggers the need" to time your outreach. A clinic opening a
  second location is a far better lead than one that's quiet.
- Use "where they spend time" to choose your lead sources (see
  lead-sources.md).

# Where to Find Clients

Ten lead sources, from warmest to coldest. Warm leads already know or trust
you, so they reply more often and decide faster. Work from the top down,
and only move to cold outreach once the warm list is exhausted.

| # | Source | Effort | How fast it pays off | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Past clients | Low | Days to weeks | Everyone |
| 2 | People who referred you before | Low | Weeks | Everyone |
| 3 | Current clients (more work, or referrals) | Low | Days to weeks | Anyone with an active client |
| 4 | Your existing network | Low-medium | Weeks | Anyone who's worked in an industry |
| 5 | Complementary freelancers and agencies | Medium | 1-3 months | Specialists who fit into bigger projects |
| 6 | Communities where your clients gather | Medium | 1-3 months | People with a clear niche |
| 7 | Speaking, workshops, guest posts | High | 2-6 months | Building authority in a niche |
| 8 | Your own published work | High | 3-12 months | Long-term inbound |
| 9 | Freelance marketplaces and job boards | Medium | Days to weeks | Filling gaps; early-career |
| 10 | Cold outreach to well-chosen prospects | Medium-high | 1-2 months | Specific, well-researched targets |

## Warm first: the list to work through before anything else

1. **Every client from the last two years.** A short, specific check-in
   (email 1 in outreach-emails.md) often turns up work that was about to go
   to someone else.
2. **Every person who has ever referred you.** Thank them and tell them
   what you're looking for now (email 3).
3. **Your current clients.** Ask what's coming up next quarter, and whether
   other teams or contacts have similar needs.
4. **Former colleagues and managers** who now work at organisations that
   fit your profile.

Most freelancers have 20-60 warm contacts. Work through all of them before
writing a single cold email.

## Notes on each source

**Complementary freelancers and agencies.** Think about who works with
your clients just before or just after you. A web designer needs a
copywriter; a copywriter needs a designer; a bookkeeper meets business
owners who need a virtual assistant. Agree to pass work both ways.

**Communities.** Join two or three places where your ideal client asks
questions (industry associations, local business groups, online forums for
their trade). Spend the first month answering questions helpfully, with no
pitch. People hire the person who was useful.

**Speaking and writing.** Slow but compounding. One short talk to a room of
the right people can be worth months of cold email. Offer a practical
30-minute session to a local business group or association.

**Your own published work.** Case studies of finished projects are the
single most useful thing to publish. One page per project: the problem,
what you did, the result in numbers if you have them (with the client's
permission).

**Marketplaces and job boards.** Useful for filling a gap quickly, but you
compete mainly on price. Use them deliberately, set a floor rate, and try
to move good clients to a direct relationship over time (where the
platform's rules allow it).

**Cold outreach.** Works when it's specific: a real person, a real trigger,
a real reason you're writing to them and not 200 others. Ten researched
emails beat 200 generic ones. Follow the privacy and anti-spam rules where
you and the recipient are based: write to business contacts about their
business, say who you are, and stop when asked.

## Pick your mix

Choose three sources to focus on this quarter and write them here:

1.
2.
3.

A good default for most freelancers: past clients and network (1-4),
one partnership source (5), and one community (6).
files.outreach-emails.md:
# Outreach Emails

Ten emails for finding new work, from warmest to coldest. Replace
everything in [brackets]. Keep them short: if an email needs scrolling on
a phone, cut it.

**Three rules for every email**

1. One clear, specific reason you're writing to *this* person now.
2. One small, easy ask (a reply, a 15-minute call), never "let me know if
   you ever need anything".
3. Nothing that could be sent unchanged to someone else.

---

## 1. Check-in with a past client

**Subject:** [Project name], six months on

Hi [Name],

I was thinking about the [project] we did in [month] and wondered how
[specific result or thing you made] has been working out. [Optional: I
noticed (something specific: a new service, a new location, a job ad).]

I've got some space opening up in [month], so if anything's on the
horizon for [area you help with], I'd be glad to help again.

Either way, I hope [something personal or business-specific] is going
well.

[Your name]

*Why it works:* it's about their result first, and it gives a concrete
reason (space opening up) without pressure.

---

## 2. Asking a happy client for a referral

Send within two weeks of a project finishing well.

**Subject:** A quick favour

Hi [Name],

Thanks again for [project]. I really enjoyed working on it, and I'm glad
[specific result].

I'm looking to work with a couple more [type of organisation] like yours
over the next few months. Is there anyone you know (a peer, a supplier, a
friend running a similar business) who might be dealing with [problem]?

If someone comes to mind, I'm happy to write a short note you can forward,
so it takes you thirty seconds.

[Your name]

---

## 3. Thanking someone who referred you before

**Subject:** Thank you, and an update

Hi [Name],

I don't think I ever properly thanked you for introducing me to [client].
We ended up [what happened], and it's been one of my favourite projects.

I'm now focusing on [your one-sentence description from the ideal client
profile]. If you come across anyone like that, I'd be grateful for an
introduction, and I'm always glad to return the favour.

[Your name]

---

## 4. Reconnecting with someone in your network

**Subject:** [Shared context]: catching up

Hi [Name],

It's been a while since [shared context: we worked together at X / met at
Y]. I saw [specific recent thing about them] and wanted to say
congratulations.

Since then I've been working as a freelance [role], mostly helping
[who] with [what]. If that ever overlaps with what you or your team need,
I'd love to hear about it. And if there's anything I can help you with,
just ask.

[Your name]

---

## 5. Proposing a referral partnership

**Subject:** Passing work both ways?

Hi [Name],

I'm a freelance [role] working mostly with [type of client]. I've seen
your work on [specific project] and noticed we often serve the same kind
of client from different sides: I do [your part], you do [their part].

Clients regularly ask me for someone who does [their service]. Would you
be open to a 20-minute call to see if it makes sense to recommend each
other?

[Your name]

---

## 6. Warm introduction request (to a mutual contact)

**Subject:** Could you introduce me to [Name]?

Hi [Mutual contact],

I noticed you're connected to [Name] at [organisation]. They look like
exactly the kind of client I work with: [one specific reason].

Would you be comfortable introducing us? I've written a short blurb below
you can forward as-is, and I completely understand if it isn't a good
fit.

> [Your name] is a freelance [role] who helps [who] [get what result].
> Recently they [one concrete project or result]. I thought you two should
> talk.

Thank you,
[Your name]

---

## 7. Cold pitch with a specific trigger

Only send this when you have a real, specific reason to write.

**Subject:** [Their trigger event]

Hi [Name],

Congratulations on [trigger: opening a second location / the new product
line / the role]. [One sentence showing you looked: a specific observation
about their website, product or announcement.]

I help [who] with [what], and when businesses [trigger], [the problem]
usually comes up. For [similar client or anonymised example], I [what you
did], which [result].

Would a 15-minute call next week be useful? If the timing's wrong, no
problem at all.

[Your name]
[One-line signature with a link to your portfolio]

---

## 8. Follow-up 1 (5-7 days after no reply)

**Subject:** Re: [original subject]

Hi [Name],

Just bringing this back to the top of your inbox in case it got buried.
[One new, useful thing: a short idea for them, a relevant example, or an
observation you didn't include before.]

Happy to send a couple of ideas by email instead of a call if that's
easier.

[Your name]

---

## 9. Follow-up 2, the polite close (7-10 days after follow-up 1)

**Subject:** Re: [original subject]

Hi [Name],

I don't want to keep filling your inbox, so this is my last note on this.
If [problem] becomes a priority later, I'd be glad to help. You can reply
to this email any time.

All the best with [specific thing].

[Your name]

*After this, stop.* Add a reminder in the tracker to check in again in
3-6 months only if a new, real trigger appears.

---

## 10. Reply to "not right now"

**Subject:** Re: [original subject]

Hi [Name],

Thanks for letting me know, I appreciate the reply. Would it be all right
if I checked back in around [month they mentioned, or three months from
now]?

In the meantime, [optional: one small useful thing: a short tip, a
checklist, an idea for their situation].

[Your name]

*Then:* set next_action_date in the tracker to that month, and actually
follow up. Most freelancers never do, which is why it works.
files.pipeline-maths.md:
# Pipeline Maths

How many people do you need to talk to each month to hit your income
target? Fill in the blanks, then compare with the worked example.

## The four numbers you need

1. **Monthly income target from new work** ($): the part of your income
   not already covered by retainers or booked projects.
2. **Average project value** ($): look at your last 5-10 projects.
3. **Win rate** (%): out of proposals or quotes sent, how many were signed.
   If you don't know, use 30%.
4. **Proposal rate** (%): out of people you had a real conversation with,
   how many asked for a proposal. If you don't know, use 40%.

And one more for outreach:

5. **Reply rate** (%): out of people you contacted, how many replied and
   had a conversation. Estimate separately: warm contacts often 20-40%,
   well-researched cold emails often 3-10%. Your own tracker will soon give
   you real numbers.

## The calculation

```
Projects needed per month      = income target / average project value
Proposals needed per month     = projects needed / win rate
Conversations needed per month = proposals needed / proposal rate
Contacts needed per month      = conversations needed / reply rate
```

Round every result **up**.

## Your numbers

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Income target from new work | $ |
| Average project value | $ |
| Projects needed per month | |
| Win rate | % |
| Proposals needed per month | |
| Proposal rate | % |
| Conversations needed per month | |
| Reply rate (warm / cold mix) | % |
| Contacts needed per month | |
| Contacts needed per week (monthly / 4.33) | |

## Worked example

A freelance designer wants $4,000 a month from new projects. Their average
project is $1,600.

| Step | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Projects needed | 4,000 / 1,600 = 2.5 | **3 projects** |
| Proposals needed | 3 / 0.35 win rate = 8.6 | **9 proposals** |
| Conversations needed | 9 / 0.45 proposal rate = 20 | **20 conversations** |
| Contacts (all warm, 30% reply) | 20 / 0.30 = 66.7 | 67 contacts |
| Contacts (all cold, 6% reply) | 20 / 0.06 = 333 | 334 contacts |
| Contacts (half warm, half cold) | 10 / 0.30 + 10 / 0.06 = 33.3 + 166.7 | **200 contacts** |

**What this tells them:**

- Relying only on cold outreach would mean ~80 emails a week. Not
  realistic, and the quality would drop.
- Shifting the mix toward warm leads cuts the work dramatically. With 75%
  warm and 25% cold: 15 / 0.30 + 5 / 0.06 = 50 + 84 = 134 contacts a month,
  about 31 a week (134 / 4.33 weeks).
- Raising the average project value has the biggest effect of all. At
  $2,400 per project they need 2 projects, 6 proposals, 14 conversations,
  and about 30% less outreach for the same income.

## Three levers, in order of impact

1. **Raise average project value**: package services, offer three options
   (with the middle one as the default), add a retainer.
2. **Raise the reply rate**: more warm leads, better triggers, more
   specific emails.
3. **Raise the win rate**: qualify better (use the walk-away signs in your
   ideal client profile) and follow up on every proposal.

Recalculate once a month using real numbers from pipeline-tracker.csv.

files.weekly-prospecting-routine.md:
# Weekly Prospecting Routine

Three hours a week, split into short blocks so it survives busy weeks.
Book these blocks in your calendar as recurring appointments.

## The week at a glance

| Day | Block | Time | What you do |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monday | Plan | 30 min | Review tracker, pick this week's contacts, set targets |
| Tuesday | Warm outreach | 40 min | Past clients, network, referral asks |
| Wednesday | Research and cold outreach | 40 min | Find triggers, write specific pitches |
| Thursday | Follow-ups | 30 min | Every lead with a next action due this week |
| Friday | Visibility and review | 40 min | Share something useful, update numbers |

## Monday: Plan (30 min)

- [ ] Open pipeline-tracker.csv and sort by next_action_date.
- [ ] Move anything stale: if a lead has had two follow-ups and no reply,
      mark it "Closed - no reply" with a note.
- [ ] Check this week's target from pipeline-maths.md (contacts per week).
- [ ] Choose names for Tuesday and Wednesday and add them to the tracker
      with stage "To contact".
- [ ] Write down one current client you'll ask for more work or a referral
      this week.

## Tuesday: Warm outreach (40 min)

- [ ] Send 3-5 emails from the warm list (emails 1-6 in
      outreach-emails.md).
- [ ] Personalise each one: one specific detail per email, minimum.
- [ ] Log each in the tracker the moment you send it, with a next action
      date 5-7 days out.

## Wednesday: Research and cold outreach (40 min)

- [ ] Spend 20 minutes finding prospects with a real trigger (new location,
      new hire, launch, rebrand, funding, busy season coming).
- [ ] Spend 20 minutes writing 2-4 cold pitches (email 7). Quality over
      quantity: if you can't find a specific reason to write, skip them.
- [ ] Log each in the tracker.

## Thursday: Follow-ups (30 min)

- [ ] Send every follow-up due this week (emails 8-10).
- [ ] Follow up on every open proposal older than five working days.
- [ ] For every "not now", confirm the check-back date is in the tracker.

## Friday: Visibility and review (40 min)

- [ ] 20 min: share one useful thing where your ideal clients are: answer a
      question in a community, post a short case study or tip, or send a
      helpful note to a referral partner.
- [ ] 20 min: weekly review (below).

### Weekly review

| This week | Number |
|---|---|
| New contacts | |
| Replies | |
| Conversations / calls | |
| Proposals sent | |
| Projects won | |
| Value won ($) | |

- What got the most replies this week, and why?
- Which source is working best so far?
- One thing to change next week:

## When you're fully booked

Don't stop. Drop to a **one-hour minimum week**: Monday plan (15 min),
Thursday follow-ups (30 min), and one warm email on Friday (15 min). Book
new projects for later start dates. This is the habit that ends the
feast-and-famine cycle.

## When work is slow

Add a second Tuesday block and work through the whole warm list before
anything else. Slow months are also the best time to write a case study
or offer a free talk to a group of ideal clients.
